claim: Early-life microbiota has been linked to the development of chronic inflammatory diseases.
source: Early-life microbiota has been linked to the development of chronic inflammatory diseases.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific literature.

claim: Maternal vaginal microbiota is hypothesized to be an important initial seeding source with potential lifelong effects on disease risk.
source: It has been hypothesized that maternal vaginal microbiota is an important initial seeding source and therefore might have lifelong effects on disease risk.
evidence: This is a hypothesis statement presented in the abstract.

claim: The study analyzed 665 mother-child dyads from the COPSAC2010 cohort.
source: To understand maternal vaginal microbiota's role in seeding the child's microbiota and the extent of delivery mode-dependent transmission, we studied 665 mother–child dyads from the COPSAC2010 cohort.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design and sample size.

claim: Maternal vaginal microbiota was evaluated twice in the third trimester.
source: The maternal vaginal microbiota was evaluated twice in the third trimester and compared with the children's fecal (at 1 week, 1 month, and 1 year of age) and airway microbiota (at 1 week, 1 month, and 3 months).
evidence: This describes the sampling protocol used in the study.

claim: Delivery mode affects the development of the microbiota in early life.
source: Delivery mode affects the development of the microbiota in early life, and differences between the microbiota of infants delivered vaginally and by cesarean section (CS) have been identified as late as at 1 year of age (Azad et al., 2013; Bäckhed et al., 2015; Stokholm et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Bacterial colonization in early life has been correlated with the risk of several chronic inflammatory disorders.
source: Such bacterial colonization in early life has been correlated with the risk of several chronic inflammatory disorders (Bisgaard et al., 2007; Bisgaard et al., 2008; Bisgaard et al., 2011; Stokholm et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Correlations have been observed between cesarean section and increased risk of chronic inflammatory diseases.
source: correlations have been observed between CS and increased risk of such diseases (Mueller et al., 2017; Sevelsted et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The vaginal microbiota of pregnant women has decreased diversity compared to non-pregnant women.
source: The vaginal microbiota of pregnant women, in comparison with non-pregnant women, has decreased diversity and increased stability (Aagaard et al., 2012; Dominguez-Bello et al., 2010; Hernández-Rodríguez et al., 2011; Romero et al., 2014; Walther-António et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The vaginal microbiota of pregnant women has increased stability compared to non-pregnant women.
source: The vaginal microbiota of pregnant women, in comparison with non-pregnant women, has decreased diversity and increased stability (Aagaard et al., 2012; Dominguez-Bello et al., 2010; Hernández-Rodríguez et al., 2011; Romero et al., 2014; Walther-António et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Five vaginal community state types (CSTs) have been identified in studies of the vaginal microbiota.
source: Several studies of the vaginal microbiota have identified five vaginal community state types (CSTs): four that are dominated by a specific Lactobacillus species and have low alpha diversity, as well as one containing facultative and strictly anaerobic bacteria, with higher alpha diversity, dominated either by Gardnerella spp. or by Gardnerella spp. with a higher amount of Lactobacillus spp. (Chaban et al., 2014; Drell et al., 2013; Gajer et al., 2012; Hyman et al., 2005; Ling et al., 2010; Ravel et al., 2011; Ravel et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2004; Zhou et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The study successfully sequenced 1322 vaginal samples from gestational weeks 24 and 36.
source: We successfully sequenced 1322 vaginal samples from gestational weeks 24 (n = 657) and 36 (n = 665), with a mean read count of 53,875 (interquartile range [IQR]: 38,330–64,632)
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sequencing results.

claim: The vaginal samples contained 3287 unique Amplicon sequence variants (ASVs).
source: We successfully sequenced 1322 vaginal samples from gestational weeks 24 (n = 657) and 36 (n = 665), with a mean read count of 53,875 (interquartile range [IQR]: 38,330–64,632), representing 3287 unique Amplicon sequence variants (ASVs)
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sequencing results.

claim: The mean observed richness in vaginal samples was 25.0 (IQR: 12–32).
source: representing 3287 unique Amplicon sequence variants (ASVs), with a mean observed richness of 25.0 (IQR: 12–32).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the alpha diversity measurement.

claim: 28 unique phyla were observed in the vaginal samples.
source: We observed 28 unique phyla, of which 10 had a mean abundance above 0.1%, and the most abundant phyla were Firmicutes (85.2%), Actinobacteria (12.0%), and Proteobacteria (1.5%).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the taxonomic composition.

claim: Firmicutes was the most abundant phylum in vaginal samples at 85.2%.
source: the most abundant phyla were Firmicutes (85.2%), Actinobacteria (12.0%), and Proteobacteria (1.5%).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the taxonomic composition.

claim: 463 genera were observed in the vaginal samples.
source: We observed 463 genera, 94 with mean abundance above 0.1%, and dominated by Lactobacillus (81.1%) and Gardnerella (9.0%).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the taxonomic composition.

claim: Lactobacillus dominated the vaginal samples at 81.1%.
source: We observed 463 genera, 94 with mean abundance above 0.1%, and dominated by Lactobacillus (81.1%) and Gardnerella (9.0%).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the taxonomic composition.

claim: The vaginal samples were clustered into six clusters.
source: We clustered the vaginal samples into six clusters (Supplementary file 1, section 1.3.1), and based on the dominant ASVs in each cluster, we refer to them as CST I (L. crispatus), CST II (L. gasseri), CST III (L. iners), CST IV-a (G. vaginalis, few Lactobacillus), CST IV-b (G. vaginalis, some Lactobacillus), and CST V (L. jensenii), in accordance with Gajer et al., 2012 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the clustering analysis results.

claim: The observed richness differed significantly between CSTs (p<10−15).
source: The observed richness differed significantly between CSTs (p<10−15, Figure 1B)
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical analysis results with reference to a figure.

claim: CST I and CST III had the lowest observed richness among the CSTs.
source: The observed richness differed significantly between CSTs (p<10−15, Figure 1B), being lowest in CSTs I, slightly higher in CST III and CST V, while CST IV-a and CST IV-b had the highest observed richness.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the alpha diversity patterns with reference to a figure.

claim: CST IV-a and CST IV-b had the highest observed richness among the CSTs.
source: being lowest in CSTs I, slightly higher in CST III and CST V, while CST IV-a and CST IV-b had the highest observed richness.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the alpha diversity patterns.

claim: Shannon diversity index was significantly different between CSTs (p<10−15).
source: Similarly, for Shannon diversity index, CST I and CST III were significantly lower than the rest, while CST IV-a and CST IV-b were also significantly higher than CST II and CST V (p<10−15, Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1, section 1.3.2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical analysis results with reference to a figure.

claim: 85.5% of women had the same CST at week 36 as they had at week 24.
source: Of the 657 women with both week 24 and 36 data, 562 (85.5%) had the same CST at week 36, as they had at week 24
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stability analysis results.

claim: CST IV-b was significantly less stable (60.0%) compared to other CSTs.
source: with CST IV-b (21 of 35–60.0%) being significantly less stable (χ2 test, adjusted p-value<0.048), except CST IV-a (30 of 45–66.7%) and CST V (26 of 39–66.7%)
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical analysis results.

claim: CST I and CST III were the most stable CSTs (92.5% and 91.1%, respectively).
source: while CST I and CST III were the most stable (92.5% and 91.1%, respectively) (Figure 1, Supplementary file 1, section 1.3.2.3.2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stability analysis results with reference to a figure.

claim: The median Jensen–Shannon divergence between women's paired week 24 and week 36 samples (0.031) was significantly lower than the median JSD between mismatched pairs (0.635) (p<10−3).
source: The median Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) between women's paired week 24 and week 36 samples (medianJSDpairs = 0.031) was significantly lower than the median JSD between mismatched pairs of week 24 and week 36 samples (medianJSDnonpairs = 0.635) (p<10−3).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical analysis results.

claim: 1746 airway samples were collected from infants with a corresponding maternal week 36 sample.
source: In the 1746 airway samples from the infants with a corresponding maternal week 36 sample (1 week: 526, 1 month: 606 and 3 months: 614), we identified 7500 ASVs

source: In the 1746 airway samples from the infants with a corresponding maternal week 36 sample (1 week: 526, 1 month: 606 and 3 months: 614), we identified 7500 ASVs

source: from 35 phyla, of which 8 had a relative abundance above 0.1%, dominated by Firmicutes (61%), Proteobacteria (30%), Actinobacteria (6%), and Bacteroidetes (2%).

source: The mean observed richness increased significantly from 1 week (16.6) to 1 month (20.5) and 3 months (25.1) (adjusted p<10−15, Figure 2B)

source: Interestingly, when sequentially adding time points followed by delivery mode or mother's CST to the analysis, both did significantly explain an additional small fraction of the beta diversity (delivery mode: R2 = 0.004, p<0.001, mother's CST: R2 = 0.007, p<0.001) (Supplementary file 1, section 2.3.4).

source: Of the 92 samples from children containing this Ureaplasma ASV, 67 (70.7 %) of the matching samples from the mother shared the ASV (Supplementary file 1, section 3.1.2.3).

source: By correlating the OR for transfer for each ASV with the population-wide relative maternal abundance, we revealed a negative correlation between maternal abundance of an ASV and the OR for transfer to the fecal compartment for vaginally (1 week: p=0.047, 1 month: p=0.0001, 1 year: p=0.0024) and CS-born children at 1 year (p<0.015)
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical analysis results.

claim: There was no association between population abundance and transfer odds to the airway (p>0.07).
source: whereas there was no association between population abundance and transfer odds to the airway (p>0.07).

source: For CS-born children, enrichment was observed for the fecal compartment at the early time point (WTRCS = 2.6 for transfer, p=0.014), but not at the later time points (WTRCS: 0.9 and 1.6, p>0.2, Figure 4).

source: Interestingly, transfer to the airway compartment was significantly enriched at the first two time points for vaginally born children, but strongest at the age of 1 month (1 week: WTRVAG = 2.3, p=0.034, 1 month: WTRVAG = 3.4, p<0.001)

claim: The study performed similar clustering of the vaginal samples and identified three clear clusters (CST I, CST II, and CST III), as well as three less-defined clusters, in concordance with previous smaller North American and European studies.
source: In concordance with the previous smaller North American and European studies (MacIntyre et al., 2015 [n = 42], Ravel et al., 2013 [n = 396], Romero et al., 2014 [n = 32+22]), we performed similar clustering of the vaginal samples and identified three clear clusters (CST I, CST II, and CST III), as well as three less-defined clusters, of which two were dominated by Gardnerella (CST IV-a and CST IV-b) and one by Lactobacillus (CST V).
evidence: This is a direct statement comparing the study results to prior research.

claim: CSTs dominated by Gardnerella had higher alpha diversity and beta diversity dispersion than Lactobacillus-dominated CSTs.
source: CSTs dominated by Gardnerella had higher alpha diversity and beta diversity dispersion than Lactobacillus-dominated CSTs, as seen in prior studies (Ravel et al., 2011; Ma and Li, 2017)

claim: The median beta diversity distance between each woman's own samples was 3.8–20.6 times smaller than the median distance to other women's samples.
source: Based on the two vaginal sampling times, we saw a high intraindividual similarity, with the median beta diversity distance between each woman's own samples being 3.8–20.6 times smaller than the median distance to other women's samples, for weighted UniFrac distances and Jensen–Shannon divergence, respectively
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data analysis results.

claim: The vaginal microbiome at week 36 is a relevant proxy for the vaginal bacteria that infants were exposed to during vaginal birth.
source: While our two sample points do not provide an in-depth proof of vaginal microbiota's stability, the high intraindividual stability was sufficient to consider the vaginal microbiota at week 36 as a relevant proxy for the vaginal bacteria that infants were exposed to during vaginal birth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stability data.

claim: The week 36 vaginal microbiota explained a small fraction of the variation in beta diversity for the children's fecal microbiome.
source: We have not found correlations with children's airway microbiome, but the week 36 vaginal microbiota did explain a small fraction of the variation in beta diversity for the children's fecal microbiome.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical analysis results.

claim: Studies investigating transfer at strain level have shown that specific bacteria are transferred from mother to infant, but none have included statistical tests that confirm the significance of the observed transfer.
source: Studies employing metagenome sequencing have investigated strain-level transfer between mother and infants; Asnicar et al., 2017 showed the feasibility of using metagenomics to identify shared bacterial strains between mother and infant, 3 months post-birth, in a handful of pairs, Ferretti et al., 2018 showed that bacterial strains from mothers' stool appear more frequently in the infants' gut microbiota at a later age, and Shao et al., 2019 showed that strain-level transmission of especially Bacteroidetes was stunted for CS-delivered children compared to vaginally delivered children. These studies all identify specific strains that show transfer between mother and infant. However, the high inter-individual variability in airway and fecal microbiomes, as well as the large differences when comparing them to the vaginal microbiome, makes it difficult to determine any statistical significance of such transfer.
evidence: This is a statement about prior research with citations and a critique of their methods.

claim: The study suggests a novel strategy for statistically testing for bacteria being consistently transferred from mother to infant, which is based on the calculation of weighted transfer ratios (WTRs) at higher taxonomic levels.
source: We therefore suggest a novel strategy for statistically testing for bacteria being consistently transferred from mother to infant, which is based on the calculation of weighted transfer ratios (WTRs) at higher taxonomic levels.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The study found only very small correlations between the vaginal microbiome at week 36 and the fecal microbiome during the first year of life.
source: With the assumption that the vaginal microbiome present at week 36 is indicative of the vaginal microbiome at birth, we found no overall correlation with the airway microbiome during the first 3 months after birth and only very small correlations with the fecal microbiome during the first year of life.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: The study found minimal evidence of ASV-specific transfer from mothers' vaginal microbiome when stratifying for time point and delivery mode to calculate the transfer odds for individual ASVs.
source: Stratifying for time point and delivery mode to calculate the transfer odds for individual ASVs, we found minimal evidence of ASV-specific transfer from mothers' vaginal microbiome.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: By comparing the development of WTR over time between delivery modes, the study can identify patterns that suggest evidence of orders that are persistently or transiently transferred during delivery, as well as orders that are shared between mother and child at a later time point.
source: To assess whether bacterial taxa were consistently transferred, we introduce the concept of weighted transfer ratios, and by comparing the development of WTR, over time, between delivery modes, we can identify patterns that suggest evidence of orders that are persistently or transiently transferred during delivery, as well as orders that are shared between mother and child at a later time point.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's methodological contribution and findings.
